text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed sharply higher although the day ended with pared gains. There were no fresh fundamental news except reports of cold weather in Brazil, which, however, is not likely to cause any damage. May added $44 to close at $1,764 per tonne, while July closed $40 higher at $1,815 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York showed further massive gains with front month May adding 15.35 cents/lb to close at 261.00 cents/lb while July closed 11.50 cents/lb higher at 241.15 cents. The sharp rise in May reasserted the May/July switch. There were no fresh fundamental news but continued fears of supply tightness pushed prices higher.

Adding to the fear was the first hint of cold weather in Brazil on a 10 day forecast. Although Weather Services indicated that a chance of frost was virtually none at this time, talk of weather was a reminder of the 50 cent ranges the market traded in 1994 following frosts and this made it all the more tempting for speculators to jump onto the bandwagon, traders said. The rise in coffee prices is really breath-taking and it should be remembered that the market is not a one-way street. Hence, corrections could be extremely violent, especially since it appears that there are ample longs getting in from levels that in the past would be considered attractive sales.
F. O. LICHT - Our second estimate of world coffee production 1996/97 will be released on Thursday, May 15, at 14.00 GMT.
UNITED STATES - The CSCE reported certified coffee stocks increased by 1,745 60-kg bags to 33,037 bags as of May 12. There were 16,435 bags of coffee pending grading, the exchange said.

COLOMBIA - Jorge Cardenas, the head of Colombian's National Coffee Growers Federation, said the country was having enormous difficulties meeting its export commitments because of unusually tight supply. He added there has been a delay in shipments for April and acknowledged that the country had fallen behind on its export schedules. He said the Federation and private exporters had planned to ship a combined total of 900,000 60-kg bags of coffee in April, but this may have been unrealistic given average shipments of no more than 800,000 bags over the past few months. Cardenas said he hoped Colombia's supply problems would ease by October.

POLAND - Poland imported 143,738 bags of coffee in November 1996, nearly 14 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 1.511 mn bags, nearly 7 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 rose by 6.47 per cent to 1.536 mn bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/November 1996 were Ivory Coast (204,000 vs 196,700 bags), Colombia (113,000 vs 62,200 bags), Peru (122,100 vs 129,800 bags), India (179,200 vs 117,700 bags), Indonesia (348,100 vs 184,500 bags) and Vietnam (157,300 vs 247,800 bags).

The country exported 83,400 bags of coffee in January/November 1996 which compares to 40,600 bags exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar 1995 reached 42,300 bags, up from 17,000 in 1994.
